newsitem.title: THAILAND: Insurance issue seen as Thai government test.
newsitem.headline: Insurance issue seen as Thai government test.

text.p: The new Thai government's promise to hold a graft-free review of contentious proposals to open up the protected Thai insurance industry won cautious praise from insurers on Thursday.

The review also looks set to be closely watched as a test of the Chavalit Yongchaiyudh administration's determination to clean up the general process of government, and liberalisation of industry, which was dogged by accusations of bribery during the term of the previous government.

Announcing the review on Wednesday, Commerce Minister Narongchai Akranasee warned that the committee set up to reconsider the stalled issuance of new insurance licences would not tolerate "lobbying" from interested parties.
His comments were backed by Finance Minister Amnuay Virawan, who said the government wanted preventative measures to limit opportunities for corruption.
Last year the issuance of new banking licences was halted pending an investigation into alleged graft.

In addition, the size and composition of a 66-strong shortlist for new life and non-life insurance firms produced by the commerce ministry last January was widely thought to have been influenced by vested interests.

"Certainly (Narongchai) was very frank that there would be no money paid and no influence on the panel, implying that this had been the practice in the past," said Peter Francke, president of Ayudhya Jardine CMG Life.
"It (corruption) is always something under the surface which damages the economy more than people realise and it's a target worth hitting pretty strongly," Francke said.
The composition of the nine-member review committee was widely praised as beyond the influence of vested interests.

Chairing the panel will be the President of the Exim Bank of Thailand, Pridiyathorn Devkula. Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanonda and two leading academics are also included, with senior civil servants making up the balance.
"This should be cautiously welcomed... They seem like competent people, they are making all the right sounds," said Chartri Panit, assistant general manager at General Accident Insurance Thailand.
Narongchai said the review would be completed and new licences issued during the first quarter of this year.
Industry executives said they expect only between 10 and 30 new licences to be granted.

Such a reduction in the number of new market entrants would be popular with executives. They believe the 101 billion baht ($4.04 billion) market, estimated to have grown 15 percent last year, can accommodate new operators but fear the granting of 66 licences would swamp the market.
"From yesterday's meeting, from what he said I think Chavalit seems to mean business, but we now have to wait and see what actions they take," Chartri said.
"We still have to see, you can never be 100 percent confident about this sort of thing here," said Francke.
